extracted.intended_audience: Congress, Department of the Interior / Bureau of Indian Affairs officials, Indian agents and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for the administration of Indian agencies, reservations, education, rations, land settlements, and related federal actions as described in an 1880 annual report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for payment under Ute agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: No payment will be made to the White River Utes until the surrender or apprehension of those members implicated in the murder of Agent Meeker and the outrages of Sept. 29, 1879; or until the President is satisfied that the guilty parties are no longer living or have fled beyond the limits of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment under the agreement is explicitly conditional on either apprehension/surrender of the guilty or Presidential satisfaction that they are dead or gone; funds appropriated under section 9 were to be paid once this condition was certified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification requirement for tribal agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement required ratification by three-fourths of the adult male Indians of the Ute tribe within four months of approval (limited to Oct. 15, 1880).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural limit on ratification period: must be certified within statutory time frame; ratification events and certification recorded by the Secretary of the Interior/Treasury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey and location prerequisite for relocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys contemplated by the act are necessary for the location of the Indians; locating operations are to follow surveys and may be seasonally constrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays in passage of enabling legislation may delay surveys and thereby suspend locating operations until appropriate seasons (e.g., next spring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Land surrender / payment terms (Fort Hall / Lemhi agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In consideration of cession, the United States agrees to pay the Lemhi Indians $4,000 per annum for 20 years and the Fort Hall Indians $6,000 per annum for 20 years, to survey and allot lands in severalty, and to issue patents with restrictive clauses against alienation when laws are passed by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement terms are contingent on Congressional acceptance and enactment of necessary laws; portions become inoperative if the tribe declines to remove (e.g., Lemhi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issuance contingent on laws and surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Lands of reservations agreed to be surveyed and allotted in severalty and patents issued with restrictive clauses against alienation 'so soon as the necessary laws are passed by Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and allotments precede patents; statutory authority is required before patents with restrictive clauses can be issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation on suitable lands for education and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Little can be effected in educational and religious interests until the tribe is consolidated upon suitable lands and brought under the controlling influence of the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation that legislation be passed to enable consolidation—consolidation is a precondition for effective schooling and agent oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation as alternative to supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mission Indians request a reservation 'upon which they can earn a subsistence for themselves and families' rather than simply receiving supplies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: providing land/reservation is preferred to repeated supply issues to enable self-support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-support measurement and ration policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-support is gauged by proportion of subsistence derived from government rations (examples: 35%, 20%, 25% at certain agencies) and by agricultural output per member; when self-support is nearly reached, issue of rations (except to aged and helpless) may cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with crops that could 'furnish ample support,' allowances must be made for 'Indian appetite and Indian improvidence' and perceived government discrimination; political judgment required before discontinuing rations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty education obligations and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under treaty obligations (example: Pawnees), the United States agrees to establish specified manual-labor boarding schools and the tribe agrees that every child aged seven to eighteen shall be kept at these schools for at least nine months each year; chiefs are responsible for attendance and failure may be punishable by deduction from annuities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School establishment numbers may be adjusted by the President; enforcement mechanisms include holding chiefs responsible and financial penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: School system design: boarding plus neighborhood day schools
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-organized system combining central boarding schools with neighborhood day schools (four day schools tied to a central boarding school) will exert a more powerful and rapid influence than boarding schools alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Day schools staffed by teachers who also look after general interests serve as 'civilizing centers'; funds for boarding schools alone are insufficient to meet demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for homestead/pre-emption eligibility after Executive reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where townships were set apart as a reservation by Executive order, Indians could initiate homestead claims only on portions of the townships set aside for their use that were not, at the date of the Executive order, occupied by whites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local investigation (with agent and Indians) to ascertain extent/character of improvements and which portions remained available; prior filings by whites (homestead, pre-emption) affect Indian rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land title confirmation needed for permanent improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the tract occupied is confirmed to Indians by act of Congress (i.e., secure title), they will be slow to settle down and make permanent improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure legal title by Congressional confirmation is a policy prerequisite for encouraging investment and development by tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for Congressional action to secure Indian locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation is recommended to provide for permanent location of tribes (example: purchase from Cherokees for Poncas) and appropriation of sums to indemnify tribes for lands and property previously owned elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory action is necessary to remove uncertainty and counteract agitators urging return/migration; implementation requires appropriation and legal purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Indian police and civil process in criminal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian police can be employed to arrest and transport offenders to proper civil authorities; offenders were to be held and turned over to civil jurisdiction (e.g., sent to Fort Randall subject to governor's requisition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example emphasizes combining patience, firmness, and kindness; cooperation from chiefs and Indian police facilitated safe transport without serious trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of violent incidents to preserve peace and satisfy parties
rubrics_metrics.description: When a murder or outrage occurred, the agent sought to arrest the murderer, place the prisoner in charge of reliable citizens for delivery to the proper court, and advise Indians to return home; failure of local citizens to follow process or intervention by lawless whites could lead to lynching and further unrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt lawful detention and transfer to civil jurisdiction is preferred; military and agent cooperation can pacify potentially vengeful tribes; failure of proper civil process risks vigilante actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of agricultural and stock resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Government may issue cattle and implements to encourage stock-raising and farming; recommendation that cattle issuance continue until every deserving family is supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stock-raising is identified as an industry better suited to drought-prone areas; careful selection of deserving recipients and continued support encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued government support after self-support
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where self-support is largely reached, continued government care is required for several years: support schools, furnish employees, repair or replace implements, and keep agency buildings and machinery in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without ongoing agency machinery and occasional support, prior investments may yield only temporary and not permanent good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for stopping specific ration components
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue of any but beef rations to certain bands (e.g., Caddoes and Delawares) was stopped due to retrogression and loss of ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjustment of ration composition may be used as policy tool when tribes regress; decisions reflect behavior and perceived needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and patent issuance for Indians moved to new reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: When Indians agree to remove and select individual allotments (example: Mag-a-bob-du band moved to Crow Creek), it is hoped Congress will authorize the issue of patents for these selections so Indians may not be again deprived of their homes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: make individual selections, seek Congressional authorization for patents to secure tenure.
